new.content: Skip to content Home > Data Science For a Non-Technical Background Data Science For a Non-Technical Background From non-technical to data scientist: A comprehensive guide to learning data science skills, building a portfolio, and starting your new career with 3RI Technologies Table of Contents PriyankaS3ri May 19, 2025 2:44 pm The demand for data science professionals has grown rapidly across industries such as healthcare, finance, e-commerce, marketing, logistics, and IT services. Businesses today rely heavily on data to make decisions, improve customer experience, and predict future trends. Because of this shift, many students and working professionals from non-technical backgrounds are now exploring – Data science coourse in Pune. One of the most common questions beginners ask is: Can a non-technical person learn data science? The answer is yes. Modern learning platforms, structured mentorship, beginner-friendly tools, and practical training have made data science more accessible than ever before. Whether you come from commerce, arts, management, mechanical engineering, or another non-IT background, you can gradually build the required skills with the right roadmap and guidance. This guide explains everything you need to know about learning data science from a non-technical background, including skills, career paths, learning roadmap, challenges, and training opportunities in Pune. Can a Non-Technical Person Learn Data Science? Many learners assume data science is only for programmers or computer science graduates. In reality, companies today value analytical thinking, business understanding, communication skills, and problem-solving abilities just as much as coding knowledge. A non-technical learner may initially find programming and statistics unfamiliar, but these concepts can be learned step-by-step through proper training and practice. Why Data Science Is No Longer Limited to IT Professionals Earlier, data-related roles were highly technical and mostly handled by software engineers. Today, businesses need professionals who can interpret data and convert it into meaningful business insights. This has opened opportunities for learners from various educational backgrounds. Industries hiring data professionals now include: Banking and finance Healthcare Retail and e-commerce Digital marketing Manufacturing Education Logistics and supply chain Professionals with domain knowledge often have an advantage because they understand industry-specific problems. Common Myths about Data science for Non-Technical Myth 1: “I need advanced coding skills.”Most beginner-level data science courses start with basic programming concepts and gradually move to advanced topics. Myth 2: “Mathematics needs to be extremely strong.” You need foundational statistics and logical thinking, not advanced theoretical mathematics. Myth 3: “Only engineers can become data scientists.” Many successful data professionals come from commerce, economics, business, and science backgrounds. Myth 4: “It is too late to switch careers.” Career transition into analytics and data science is now common among working professionals. Your Roadmap to a Successful Career in Data Science Data science has been one of the most sought after areas for over a decade, and it doesn’t seem to be slowing down. According to US Bureau of Labor Statistics projections, 11.5 million Data science jobs will exist by 2026.As of early 2024, there are only 4 million available data scientists’ specialist. This graphic illustrates the notable disparity between the number of data scientists needed and those that are available. Role Primary Responsibility Beginner Friendly Data Analyst Analyze reports and dashboards Yes Business Analyst Improve business decisions using data Yes Data Scientist Build predictive models and analytics systems Moderate Machine Learning Engineer Develop AI-driven applications Advanced Data Engineer Manage data infrastructure Technical Data literacy and analysis are crucial for survival and growth in the cutthroat economy of today. The importance of data scientists to the success of contemporary businesses is directly related to its high demand. When it comes to making decisions, the most powerful firms in the world of data science career —Google, Apple, Amazon, and Facebook—all rely heavily on data. Skills Required to Learn Data Science From a Non-Technical Background Working as a Data scientist requires both Data science technical and soft skills. To work as a data scientist, one needs to possess the following abilities. Strong fundamental comprehension of mathematical ideas like probability and statistics Solid working knowledge of R or Python. Expertise in database management, including SQL and NoSQL technologies Experience with spreadsheets. Understanding of data visualization technologies like Tableau and Power BI. Solid comprehension of the principles of deep learning and machine learning Familiarity with cloud computing platforms such as GCP, AWS, or Azure A specialist in version control systems like GitHub and Git. Strong communication skills Data Analyst vs Data Scientist: What’s the Difference? S.No. Parameters Data Analyst Data Scientist 1 Definition To find useful insights, a data analyst looks at big data sets. A data scientist, on the other hand, is in charge of gathering, examining, and interpreting complicated data in order to develop prediction models and make judgments based on the data. 2 Career Scope A data analyst’s professional path usually begins with an entry-level job as a research assistant or data entry clerk. . A data scientist, on the other hand, is in charge of gathering, examining, and interpreting complicated data in order to develop prediction models and make judgments based on the data. 3 Eligibility A solid foundation in mathematics, statistics, and computer science, as well as competence with programming languages like Python and SQL, are typically prerequisites for becoming a data analyst. Additionally, data scientists need to be passionate about applying data-driven ways to solve challenging challenges and possess great communication abilities. 4 Course Duration Data analysts typically require a shorter educational path with an emphasis on basic data analysis skills. Data scientists typically require advanced degrees and deeper training in machine learning and complex statistical modeling, which results in longer course duration. 5 Demand Data Analyst has less capacity to solve more challenging issues and generate novel insights through sophisticated modeling. However, data scientists are often seen to be more in demand. 6 Top Company hiring Top organizations hiring for both professions include digital giants like Google, Amazon, and Microsoft, as well as companies in banking, healthcare, and retail sectors, Same as Data analyst, depending on the specific data demands. 7 Salary Making the appropriate decision may depend on your understanding of the income possibilities of a data science or analytics job. A data analyst makes, on average, $65,630 a year. Data scientists can earn up to $123,842 a year, according to Indeed. Step-by-Step RoadMap for Data science for Non-Technical Persons Step 1: Statistics and Probability The majority of recruiters want applicants with strong analytical skills when recruiting data scientists . You must cultivate mathematical intuition in order to acquire these abilities. Learn important statistics concepts including descriptive statistics and the normal distribution. Review the linear algebra ideas and calculus formulas that will subsequently aid in your comprehension of how machine learning algorithms are developed. Step 2: Proficiency in MS Excel Then start learning Excel. Excel is simple to learn and use thanks to its intuitive layout, even for people who are unfamiliar with data science principles. It is a great place to start when exploring and analyzing data, and it has powerful data cleansing, organizing, and manipulation tools, such as filtering, sorting, and removing duplicates. Discover important functions and formulas, such as text functions (LEFT, RIGHT, CONCATENATE), logical functions (IF, AND, OR), statistical functions (AVERAGE, MEDIAN, STANDARD DEVIATION), and lookup functions (VLOOKUP, INDEX MATCH). You should also learn how to handle missing values, eliminate duplicates, format data consistently, and identify trends with conditional formatting. Step 3: Working on Data with Power BI Data scientists have access to numerous sophisticated data visualization choices with Power BI. Among these features include smooth integration with other Microsoft products, such Excel and Azure, which facilitates team collaboration and dashboard sharing. With Power BI, you can create engaging data stories that can be used to reveal hidden trends, find correlations, or share findings with stakeholders. Next, investigate Power BI’s formula language, DAX, which allows you to perform calculations and modify data right within your visualizations. With DAX, you can build trustworthy data models that connect and manage connections between numerous data sources. Get even more inventive with the variety of visualization options available to tailor your findings for certain audiences. Want to Book A Free Expert Guidance Session? Book Now Get Free Career Counseling from Experts ! Email Phone Send Step 4: Start with Python Programming It is no coincidence that Python has emerged as the dominant language in data science. It is perfect for revealing hidden meanings in data because of its versatility, strength, and simplicity of usage. A diverse ecosystem of data science libraries, including scikit-learn, Pandas, and NumPy, provides pre-built tools for data manipulation, analysis, and machine learning. Gaining proficiency in Python programming opens up a wide range of career advancement opportunities and makes it simple to enter the data science field. Additionally, Python seamlessly integrates with other well-known data science tools, like Jupyter Notebooks and SQL databases, making the process more efficient. To begin, learn the fundamentals of Python, such as lists, tuples, and dictionaries, which form the basis for increasingly complex tasks. Next, look at Pandas, a helpful framework for data selection, cleaning, aggregation, and filtering. NumPy provides powerful tools for numerical operations and calculations on big datasets, including linear system solution and matrix multiplication. Lastly, try out visualization tools like Matplotlib and Seaborn to produce engaging data stories. Want to Book A Free Expert Guidance Session? Book Now Get Free Career Counseling from Experts ! Email Phone Send Step 5: Familiarity with Machine Learning Concepts Understanding machine learning concepts is necessary to build your toolbox because they make clear how algorithms utilize data to learn and create predictions. With this knowledge, you can create accurate forecasts, automate tasks, and glean valuable insights from raw statistics. Start by learning about supervised learning principles like regression and classification, as well as unsupervised learning ideas like clustering and dimensionality reduction. Discover model evaluation concepts like correctness, confusion matrices, and cross-validation. Once you have a solid foundation, move on to more intricate concepts like deep learning, reinforcement learning, and ensemble approaches. Step 6: Solidify your Data Management Skills Next, improve your knowledge of database administration and SQL (Structured Query Language), which will allow you to view, modify, and evaluate data in relational databases. Before analysis, data can be cleaned, modified, and filtered using SQL. Start by going over the foundations of SQL and database administration. Practice frequently on sites like LeetCode and HackerRank at the same time. With this two-pronged approach, you build a strong foundation and get closer to mastery. Step 7: Understanding Cloud Computing Platforms Data scientists are aware of the persistent challenges associated with managing constantly growing amounts of data, computationally demanding tasks, and the requirement for highly scalable resources. Thankfully, cloud computing provides a strong and adaptable substitute that can aid in resolving these issues. Cloud systems remove the limitations of on-premise hardware by enabling smooth resource scaling based on your project’s needs. The pay-as-you-go strategy is more economical since it eliminates the need for any up-front infrastructure expenditures. Start by considering familiarizing yourself with well-known cloud systems like Google Cloud Platform (GCP), Amazon Web Services (AWS), and Microsoft Azure. Your real-world experience will help you manage data sources and carry out essential tasks in cloud environments. Step 8: Experience with Version Control Systems You have to efficiently handle your code, scripts, and data as a data scientist. Working with others, keeping track of changes, and referring back to previous iterations when necessary all depend on version control systems like GitHub and Git. It’s important to maintain a detailed log of every modification you make to your code, data files, and scripts. This strategy encourages productive teamwork, enabling you to collaborate with colleagues in a fluid manner while integrating changes and averting conflicts. Learn the basic Git commands, including add, commit, push, pull, and merge, to get started. Examine further GitHub capabilities such as repositories, pull requests, branches, and version control visualisation. These resources can help you become a better team player and project manager. Step 9: Get to Work on Practical Projects This is your chance to demonstrate your abilities. Search for datasets in any field that piques your interest; the possibilities are nearly limitless, whether it be finance, music, sports, or another topic. Engage in real-world problem-solving initiatives since here is where learning by doing takes place. Finding and collecting the information required for investigation is essential before starting real-world initiatives. For this, a number of internet resources, including FiveThirtyEight, the UCI Machine Learning Repository, and Kaggle, can be helpful. By providing you with access to a range of datasets, these platforms enable you to work on pertinent projects that enhance your skills and expertise. Step 10: Networking and Collaboration There are many notable people in the data science community. Make connections with them both online and off through workshops, seminars, and a variety of online discussion boards. Think about collaborating on projects, exchanging experiences, and learning from others to hone your skills. Make the effort to set up and maintain your profile on well-known employment sites like Naukri and LinkedIn. Make sure you regularly add your relevant skills and accomplishments to your profiles. Participate on these venues by sharing your accomplishments, growth, and industry expertise. You increase your visibility to recruiters and your chances of being interviewed by doing this. Analyze data, determine how to apply it to resolve problems, get vital information about a company’s customers, and boost sales. 2 Analysis Techniques: Data scientists use more sophisticated methods like machine learning, deep learning, and statistical modeling, data analysts use more straightforward statistical analysis and data visualization tools. Analytical and statistical techniques are used to analyze, clean, convert, and model data in order to do this. 3 Business Impact: Data scientists concentrate on creating predictive models to identify future opportunities and potential risks. Can someone with a non-technical background work in data science? It is entirely possible for people with non-technical backgrounds to work in data science . Given the demand for data-savvy professionals across numerous industries, expect specialization in the field. Even while the phrase “data scientist” may evolve over time, the demand for insights based on data will only increase. 3. Can someone without any prior experience pursue a profession in data science? All that is required is a deep comprehension of the technologies and tools that data scientists use to build predictive models or help businesses use their data efficiently for forecasting the future. 4. Download Free e-Guide Machine Learning Skills You Can Learn in Machine Learning Course in Pune A well-structured Machine learning course in Pune goes far beyond theory. It equips you with practical, job-ready skills that employers actively look for. The key skills you can expect developing are broken down below: Programming and Data Handling : Python is the backbone of modern machine learning. Courses cover foundational programming concepts — functions, loops, file handling, and object-oriented programming — and build up to data manipulation using libraries like Pandas and NumPy. You also learn how to connect and manage relational databases, which is essential for working with real-world datasets. Data Preprocessing and Exploratory Analysis : Raw data is rarely clean. You learn how to handle missing values, detect outliers, normalize datasets, and perform exploratory data analysis (EDA) using tools like Matplotlib and Seaborn. These machine learning skills form the essential groundwork before any model is built. Core Machine Learning Algorithms : The curriculum revolves around this. You obtain practical experience with: Supervised Learning: Support Vector Machines (SVM), Random Forests, Decision Trees, Logistic Regression, Linear Regression, and k-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) Unsupervised Learning: K-Means Clustering, DBSCAN, and dimensionality reduction techniques like PCA Model Evaluation: Accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and cross-validation techniques to assess model reliability Deep Learning and Neural Networks : Deep learning frameworks like TensorFlow, Keras, and PyTorch are taught in advanced Machine learning classes in Pune . You learn to build multi-layer neural networks applied to image recognition, natural language processing, and time-series forecasting—capabilities that are increasingly in demand across industries. Statistical Foundations and Mathematics : ML is built on mathematics. Courses cover probability, statistics, linear algebra, and calculus—not in an abstract academic sense, but in the context of how these concepts power algorithms and model optimization. End-to-End Project Work : The best courses integrate all these skills through real-world projects. Working on datasets from domains like healthcare, e-commerce, or finance ensures you graduate with a portfolio that demonstrates practical impact — not just theoretical knowledge. A dedicated certification fills that gap with hands-on labs, capstone projects, and mentorship from working professionals. Higher Negotiating Power : Certified professionals are often able to negotiate better starting salaries. When your Machine learning certification comes with demonstrated project work and a verifiable credential, it strengthens your case in salary discussions. ML is not confined to the IT sector — it is transforming operations, decision-making, and customer experience across multiple verticals. For instance, radiologists can identify cancer faster and more accurately due to models trained on medical imaging data. E-Commerce and Retail : Recommendation engines — the technology behind “You may also like” suggestions on platforms like Amazon and Flipkart — are among the most visible applications of ML. ML is also used by retailers for dynamic pricing, supply chain optimization, and demand forecasting. Manufacturing and Industry 4.0 : Predictive maintenance is a game-changer for manufacturers. Machine learning models use sensor data from equipment to forecast faults before they happen, which significantly reduces maintenance costs and downtime. Education Technology : EdTech platforms use ML to personalize learning paths, identify students at risk of dropping out, and automate grading for certain types of assessments. Logistics and Transportation : Route optimization, delivery time prediction, and autonomous vehicle technology all rely on ML. Companies like Zomato and Swiggy in India use ML extensively to optimize delivery routes and predict demand. Pune, with its dense concentration of IT firms, fintech startups, and manufacturing companies, offers an especially rich environment to apply these skills right after completing your Machine learning course in Pune . Machine learning salaries in India grow significantly with experience. Mid-level engineers with three to five years of experience command ₹12 to 18 LPA, whereas entry-level professionals usually make between ₹5 and 8 LPA. Senior ML engineers and research scientists at top companies can earn upwards of ₹25 LPA or more. Pune-based companies in sectors including IT services, product development, and fintech are actively hiring ML professionals. Companies such as Infosys, Persistent Systems, Bajaj Finserv, and several global MNCs with Pune offices regularly post openings for ML engineers and data scientists. Strong growth trajectories are another benefit of working in machine learning. Starting as a junior ML engineer, professionals can advance to roles such as Senior Data Scientist, ML Architect, or even AI Product Manager, with each step bringing significant salary and responsibility upgrades. Conclusion The intersection of Pune’s thriving tech ecosystem and the explosive global demand for machine learning talent makes this an ideal time to invest in the right training. A quality Machine learning course in Pune builds the technical foundation—from Python and data preprocessing to deep learning and model optimization—while a recognized certification validates your capabilities to employers. The career opportunities span every industry from healthcare to logistics, and the machine learning salary in India continues to grow year on year. Table of Contents PriyankaS3ri March 20, 2025 1:19 pm Choosing the right database is one of the most critical decisions in software development, and the most common debate in the open-source world is mysql vs postgresql. While many developers weigh the mysql and postgresql differences, others come from a background in powerful enterprise solutions, often starting their journey with MS SQL Server Classes In Pune . Regardless of your starting point, understanding the fundamental difference between mysql and postgresql is vital for any tech professional. This guide will explore the postgre vs mysql comparison in detail to help you navigate the database landscape with confidence. Breaking Down the MySQL and PostgreSQL Differences In the world of databases, two of the most popular relational database management systems (RDBMS) are MySQL and PostgreSQL. Both are open-source, widely used, and powerful, yet they serve different use cases and offer distinct advantages. Choosing the right database for your application depends on factors like performance, scalability, features, and ease of use. In this blog, we will explore the key differences between MySQL and PostgreSQL, highlighting their strengths and weaknesses with real-time examples and scenarios. When it comes to database management in Data science and analytics courses in Pune , PostgreSQL and MySQL are two of the most popular choices, but their performance varies depending on project needs. PostgreSQL is preferred for complex queries, large datasets, and advanced analytics, making it highly relevant for learners exploring AI and data science courses . On the other hand, MySQL offers faster performance for simpler read-heavy applications, which is why it is widely used in web development projects. For students checking data science course eligibility or searching for a data science course near me , understanding the difference between PostgreSQL and MySQL can provide valuable insight into how real-world data is stored, managed, and analyzed. What is MySQL? MySQL is an open-source RDBMS that is widely known for its speed, simplicity, and reliability . It was originally developed by MySQL AB and later acquired by Oracle Corporation. MySQL is commonly used in web applications , such as WordPress, Joomla, and Drupal, because of its fast read performance and ease of integration. Real-Time Example: E-commerce Website Imagine you are developing an e-commerce website like Amazon. Since customers frequently perform searches, MySQL can efficiently handle high read operations with indexing . Many online stores rely on MySQL because it ensures fast retrieval of product listings while handling large volumes of transactions. What is PostgreSQL? PostgreSQL, also known as Postgres , is an advanced open-source RDBMS that is known for its extensibility, compliance with SQL standards, and support for complex queries . It is used in applications that require high data integrity, complex queries, and advanced features like JSON support and full-text search . Real-Time Example: Financial System Consider a banking system that requires transactional integrity and supports complex queries. PostgreSQL is an ideal choice because it offers ACID compliance , multi-version concurrency control (MVCC) , and support for stored procedures. A bank needs to ensure that transactions such as deposits and withdrawals are executed without data inconsistencies, making PostgreSQL a perfect fit. Key Differences Between MySQL and PostgreSQL Feature MySQL PostgreSQL Performance Faster for simple queries Optimized for complex queries SQL Compliance Partial SQL compliance Highly SQL-compliant Data Integrity Moderate High (ACID compliance by default) Scalability Horizontal scaling Vertical and horizontal scaling Extensibility Limited Highly extensible (supports custom data types and functions) JSON Support Basic JSON support Advanced JSON/JSONB support Replication Master-slave replication Multi-master replication Full-text Search Basic Advanced (supports GIN and GiST indexes) Concurrency Control Basic MVCC Advanced MVCC Usage Best for web apps, CMS, and e-commerce Best for complex applications, analytics, and financial systems 1. Performance Comparison MySQL is optimized for read-heavy operations and simple queries, while PostgreSQL performs better with write-heavy and complex queries . Scenario: Social Media Application MySQL: If you’re building a social media platform like Twitter, where users frequently fetch tweets, MySQL can efficiently handle these high-speed read operations. PostgreSQL: If you’re building a data-driven social network like LinkedIn, which requires advanced analytics, PostgreSQL would be a better fit due to its optimized query execution . 2. Data Integrity & ACID Compliance MySQL: Provides ACID compliance only when using the InnoDB storage engine . PostgreSQL: Fully ACID-compliant by default, ensuring data integrity for mission-critical applications. Unlock the Secrets to a Powerful LinkedIn Profile ! Download Free e-Guide Scenario: Healthcare Application If you’re developing a medical records system , ensuring data integrity is crucial. PostgreSQL would be a better choice because it guarantees that patient data remains consistent and prevents data corruption. 3. JSON & NoSQL Capabilities While both MySQL and PostgreSQL support JSON, PostgreSQL offers better JSON handling with JSONB , allowing efficient indexing and query execution. Scenario: Real-Time Chat Application A messaging app like WhatsApp stores messages in JSON format. PostgreSQL’s JSONB support enables faster message retrieval and structured queries, making it an ideal choice over MySQL. 4. Replication & High Availability MySQL: Supports master-slave replication , making it useful for read-heavy applications. PostgreSQL: Supports multi-master replication and provides better fault tolerance . Scenario: Cloud-Based SaaS Application If you’re running a multi-region SaaS platform , PostgreSQL’s multi-master replication ensures data consistency across regions, reducing downtime and improving user experience. 5. Full-Text Search Capabilities MySQL: Offers basic full-text search but lacks advanced indexing. PostgreSQL: Supports advanced full-text search using GIN and GiST indexes . PostgreSQL’s advanced full-text search ensures fast and accurate search results, making it a better choice. 6. Community & Licensing MySQL: Open-source but owned by Oracle , which imposes some restrictions. PostgreSQL: Completely open-source with a strong community-driven development model. Scenario: Open-Source Project If you’re developing an open-source analytics tool , PostgreSQL would be a preferable choice as it has no commercial restrictions, unlike MySQL. Choosing the Right Database for Your Needs Use Case Recommended Database Simple web applications (blogs, CMS) MySQL E-commerce platforms MySQL Financial transactions PostgreSQL Business Intelligence & Analytics PostgreSQL Large-scale applications with complex queries PostgreSQL NoSQL hybrid applications PostgreSQL Real-time applications (chat, IoT) PostgreSQL Conclusion Both MySQL and PostgreSQL have their strengths and ideal use cases. Choose MySQL if you need simplicity, speed, and easy integration for read-heavy applications. Choose PostgreSQL if you need advanced features, scalability, and complex query execution . old.content: Skip to content Home > Page Object Model (POM) and Page Factory in Selenium: Benefits & Best Practices Page Object Model (POM) and Page Factory in Selenium: Benefits & Best Practices Learn how Page Object Model (POM) and Page Factory improve the structure, reusability, and maintainability of Selenium automation frameworks. If you're exploring a Selenium Course in Pune, this guide provides practical insights and best practices to strengthen your automation testing skills. Table of Contents PriyankaS3ri July 27, 2026 2:06 pm Selenium test scripts often become messy and hard to maintain when locators and test logic are mixed together. This is where the Page Object Model and Page Factory come in, offering a structured way to organize automation code. Together, they help testers build reusable, readable, and scalable test scripts. For anyone exploring Selenium courses in Pune , understanding these design patterns is a foundational skill that separates beginner-level scripting from professional-grade automation development. Both ideas are explained in this post in a clear, useful manner. Understanding the Page Object Model (POM) in Selenium Every web page is treated as a separate class in Selenium’s Page Object Model design model. Every class contains the web elements (locators) and methods (actions) related to that specific page. Instead of writing locators repeatedly across test files, testers store them in one place, making the code easier to read and maintain. This method keeps page-specific code and test logic apart. When a developer changes a button ID or a field name, testers only need to update it in one page class rather than searching through dozens of test scripts. This single change reduces maintenance time significantly, especially in large Selenium Webdriver projects with hundreds of test cases. Core Components of a Page Object Model A well-structured Page Object Model in Selenium typically includes: Web elements : Locators such as ID, name, XPath, or CSS selectors defined as class variables. Constructor : sets up the WebDriver object for that specific class of page. Methods : Actions like clicking buttons, entering text, or verifying page elements. Page class files : Every application page has a unique class. Test class : Calls the page methods to perform actual test steps. How to Use the Page Object Model in Selenium Implementing POM is straightforward once the structure is clear: Identify the web pages involved in your test scenario. Every page should have its own Java class. Declare all locators as private variables within that class. Write public methods that perform actions using those locators. Create a separate test class that calls these methods in sequence. Validations and assertions should be kept inside the test class rather than the page class. Practical Example: Page Object Model in Selenium Consider a login page built using standard POM: The login button, password field, and username field locators are stored in a LoginPage class. The class includes methods like enterUsername(), enterPassword(), and clickLogin(). The test class simply calls loginPage.enterUsername(“test”) without worrying about how the element is located. Assertions and validations stay in the test class, keeping the page class focused only on actions. This separation keeps test scripts clean and business-focused, which is a core principle taught in any solid Selenium Classes in Pune . Understanding Page Factory in Selenium Selenium’s Page Factory is an extension of its own Page Object Model that makes element initialization easier. Page Factory employs annotations like @FindBy to declare locators directly above the variable declaration, as opposed to manually identifying items using findElement().This improves the code’s readability and clarity. Page Factory also introduces lazy initialization, meaning elements aren’t located until they are actually used in a test step, which can improve performance in certain scenarios. Page Factory Implementation in a Selenium Project To use Selenium’s Page Factory: Import the org.openqa.selenium. support. PageFactory package. Declare WebElements using the @FindBy annotation with the desired locator strategy. Initialize elements in the constructor using PageFactory.initElements(driver, this). Use these WebElements directly in methods without repeated findElement() calls. Keep the class structure similar to standard POM, just with annotation-based locators. Email Phone Send Practical Example: Page Factory in Selenium Using the same login example, rebuilt with Page Factory: The class declares @FindBy(id = “username”) WebElement usernameField instead of writing driver. findElement(By.id(“username”)) every time. The password box and login button now have similar @FindBy annotations. The constructor calls PageFactory.initElements(driver, this) to activate these elements. This small change reduces boilerplate code and makes the class visually cleaner. It’s a technique particularly helpful for beginners learning Selenium Webdriver concepts for the first time. Key Distinctions Between Page Factory and Page Object Model While Page Factory is technically built on top of POM, there are practical differences worth understanding before choosing one for your Selenium Automation Framework . Feature Page Object Model Page Factory Element Location Uses findElement() explicitly Uses @FindBy annotations Initialization Elements located each time they’re called Elements initialized via PageFactory. initElements() Code Readability Moderate, more manual code Higher, cleaner syntax Performance Standard element lookup Supports lazy loading of elements Learning Curve Easier for absolute beginners Requires understanding of annotations Flexibility More control over locator logic Slightly less flexible for dynamic locators Both approaches achieve the same goal, better-structured, maintainable code, but Page Factory offers a more streamlined syntax once testers are comfortable with annotations. Many professionals preparing for a Selenium Certification study both patterns since interview questions frequently compare the two. Benefits and Best Practices for Using POM and Page Factory Both design patterns solve real problems that testers face daily when scaling automation projects across large web applications. Key Advantages of Page Factory and POM Improved maintainability : Locator changes require updates in only one place. Code reusability : You can utilize page classes in more than one test script. Better readability : Test scripts read like plain business logic rather than technical locator strings. Reduced duplication : Common actions are written once and called repeatedly. Easier collaboration : Teams can divide work by page class, speeding up development. Scalability : Adding new test cases doesn’t require rewriting existing locators. Unlock the Secrets to a Powerful LinkedIn Profile ! Download Free e-Guide Best Practices for Building a Scalable Selenium Framework Keep locators private and expose only methods to the test layer. Avoid placing assertions inside page classes; keep them in test classes. Use meaningful, consistent naming conventions for classes and methods. Combine POM with a base class to avoid repeating WebDriver setup code. Integrate with TestNG or JUnit for structured test execution and reporting. Regularly refactor page classes as the application UI evolves. Learners who want hands-on guidance often find that structured mentorship accelerates this learning curve considerably. 3RI Technologies offers practical, project-based training that helps students apply POM and Page Factory concepts to real applications, building the kind of portfolio that stands out to employers hiring automation testers. Conclusion The fundamental issue of maintaining clean, maintainable, and scalable automation code is addressed by both the Page Object Model and Page Factory. While POM offers more manual control, Page Factory simplifies element initialization through annotations. Choosing between them, or combining both, depends on project needs and team preference. Mastering these patterns is a valuable step for anyone building a career in test automation, and structured, focused Selenium Classes in Pune can help learners apply these concepts confidently in real-world projects. Frequently Asked Questions 1. What is the primary distinction between Selenium’s Page Factory and Page Object Model? POM requires manually locating elements using findElement(), while Page Factory uses @FindBy annotations and PageFactory.initElements() for simpler, cleaner element initialization. 2. Is Page Factory better than Page Object Model? Neither is strictly better; Page Factory is an extension of POM that offers cleaner syntax, while POM gives more manual control over locator logic. Both are widely used in professional projects. 3. Do I need to learn POM before Page Factory? Yes, understanding POM fundamentals first makes it much easier to grasp how Page Factory simplifies and builds upon the same design pattern. 4. Can POM be used with TestNG and JUnit frameworks? Absolutely. POM integrates smoothly with both TestNG and JUnit, making it a standard choice for building scalable Selenium automation framework structures. 5. How does learning POM and Page Factory help my testing career? These patterns are considered essential skills in most QA automation job roles, and demonstrating proficiency in them, often validated through practical training or a Selenium Certification, can significantly improve job prospects. new.content: Skip to content Home > Page Object Model (POM) and Page Factory in Selenium: Benefits & Best Practices Page Object Model (POM) and Page Factory in Selenium: Benefits & Best Practices Learn how Page Object Model (POM) and Page Factory improve the structure, reusability, and maintainability of Selenium automation frameworks. If you're exploring a Selenium Course in Pune, this guide provides practical insights and best practices to strengthen your automation testing skills. Table of Contents PriyankaS3ri July 27, 2026 2:06 pm Selenium test scripts often become messy and hard to maintain when locators and test logic are mixed together. This is where the Page Object Model and Page Factory come in, offering a structured way to organize automation code. Together, they help testers build reusable, readable, and scalable test scripts. For anyone exploring Selenium courses in Pune , understanding these design patterns is a foundational skill that separates beginner-level scripting from professional-grade automation development. Both ideas are explained in this post in a clear, useful manner. Understanding the Page Object Model (POM) in Selenium Every web page is treated as a separate class in Selenium’s Page Object Model design model. Every class contains the web elements (locators) and methods (actions) related to that specific page. Instead of writing locators repeatedly across test files, testers store them in one place, making the code easier to read and maintain. This method keeps page-specific code and test logic apart. When a developer changes a button ID or a field name, testers only need to update it in one page class rather than searching through dozens of test scripts. This single change reduces maintenance time significantly, especially in large Selenium Webdriver projects with hundreds of test cases. Core Components of a Page Object Model A well-structured Page Object Model in Selenium typically includes: Web elements : Locators such as ID, name, XPath, or CSS selectors defined as class variables. Constructor : sets up the WebDriver object for that specific class of page. Methods : Actions like clicking buttons, entering text, or verifying page elements. Page class files : Every application page has a unique class. Test class : Calls the page methods to perform actual test steps. How to Use the Page Object Model in Selenium Implementing POM is straightforward once the structure is clear: Identify the web pages involved in your test scenario. Every page should have its own Java class. Declare all locators as private variables within that class. Write public methods that perform actions using those locators. Create a separate test class that calls these methods in sequence. Validations and assertions should be kept inside the test class rather than the page class. Practical Example: Page Object Model in Selenium Consider a login page built using standard POM: The login button, password field, and username field locators are stored in a LoginPage class. The class includes methods like enterUsername(), enterPassword(), and clickLogin(). The test class simply calls loginPage.enterUsername(“test”) without worrying about how the element is located. Assertions and validations stay in the test class, keeping the page class focused only on actions. This separation keeps test scripts clean and business-focused, which is a core principle taught in any solid Selenium Classes in Pune . Understanding Page Factory in Selenium Selenium’s Page Factory is an extension of its own Page Object Model that makes element initialization easier. Page Factory employs annotations like @FindBy to declare locators directly above the variable declaration, as opposed to manually identifying items using findElement().This improves the code’s readability and clarity. Page Factory also introduces lazy initialization, meaning elements aren’t located until they are actually used in a test step, which can improve performance in certain scenarios. Page Factory Implementation in a Selenium Project To use Selenium’s Page Factory: Import the org.openqa.selenium. support. PageFactory package. Declare WebElements using the @FindBy annotation with the desired locator strategy. Initialize elements in the constructor using PageFactory.initElements(driver, this). Use these WebElements directly in methods without repeated findElement() calls. Keep the class structure similar to standard POM, just with annotation-based locators. Email Phone Send Practical Example: Page Factory in Selenium Using the same login example, rebuilt with Page Factory: The class declares @FindBy(id = “username”) WebElement usernameField instead of writing driver. findElement(By.id(“username”)) every time. The password box and login button now have similar @FindBy annotations. The constructor calls PageFactory.initElements(driver, this) to activate these elements. This small change reduces boilerplate code and makes the class visually cleaner. It’s a technique particularly helpful for beginners learning Selenium Webdriver concepts for the first time. Key Distinctions Between Page Factory and Page Object Model While Page Factory is technically built on top of POM, there are practical differences worth understanding before choosing one for your Selenium Automation Framework . Feature Page Object Model Page Factory Element Location Uses findElement() explicitly Uses @FindBy annotations Initialization Elements located each time they’re called Elements initialized via PageFactory. initElements() Code Readability Moderate, more manual code Higher, cleaner syntax Performance Standard element lookup Supports lazy loading of elements Learning Curve Easier for absolute beginners Requires understanding of annotations Flexibility More control over locator logic Slightly less flexible for dynamic locators Both approaches achieve the same goal, better-structured, maintainable code, but Page Factory offers a more streamlined syntax once testers are comfortable with annotations. Many professionals preparing for a Selenium Certification study both patterns since interview questions frequently compare the two. Benefits and Best Practices for Using POM and Page Factory Both design patterns solve real problems that testers face daily when scaling automation projects across large web applications. Key Advantages of Page Factory and POM Improved maintainability : Locator changes require updates in only one place. Code reusability : You can utilize page classes in more than one test script. Better readability : Test scripts read like plain business logic rather than technical locator strings. Reduced duplication : Common actions are written once and called repeatedly. Easier collaboration : Teams can divide work by page class, speeding up development. Scalability : Adding new test cases doesn’t require rewriting existing locators. Avoid placing assertions inside page classes; keep them in test classes. Use meaningful, consistent naming conventions for classes and methods. Combine POM with a base class to avoid repeating WebDriver setup code. Integrate with TestNG or JUnit for structured test execution and reporting. Regularly refactor page classes as the application UI evolves. Conclusion The fundamental issue of maintaining clean, maintainable, and scalable automation code is addressed by both the Page Object Model and Page Factory. While POM offers more manual control, Page Factory simplifies element initialization through annotations. Choosing between them, or combining both, depends on project needs and team preference. Mastering these patterns is a valuable step for anyone building a career in test automation, and structured, focused Selenium Classes in Pune can help learners apply these concepts confidently in real-world projects. Frequently Asked Questions 1. What is the primary distinction between Selenium’s Page Factory and Page Object Model? POM requires manually locating elements using findElement(), while Page Factory uses @FindBy annotations and PageFactory.initElements() for simpler, cleaner element initialization. 2. Is Page Factory better than Page Object Model? Neither is strictly better; Page Factory is an extension of POM that offers cleaner syntax, while POM gives more manual control over locator logic. Both are widely used in professional projects. 3. Do I need to learn POM before Page Factory? Yes, understanding POM fundamentals first makes it much easier to grasp how Page Factory simplifies and builds upon the same design pattern. 4. Can POM be used with TestNG and JUnit frameworks? Absolutely. POM integrates smoothly with both TestNG and JUnit, making it a standard choice for building scalable Selenium automation framework structures. 5. How does learning POM and Page Factory help my testing career? These patterns are considered essential skills in most QA automation job roles, and demonstrating proficiency in them, often validated through practical training or a Selenium Certification, can significantly improve job prospects. Table of Contents PriyankaS3ri August 5, 2026 5:47 pm Is Java on its way out, or is everyone just tired of hearing about it? It’s a fair question, honestly. New languages keep stealing the spotlight, yet if you look behind the scenes of almost any banking platform, airline reservation system, or eCommerce application, you’ll still find Java powering the core. In 2026, current trends in Java technology show that the language isn’t fading—it’s evolving. With stronger cloud support, better performance, and modern development tools, Java continues to be a trusted choice for building scalable applications. That’s also why many students and working professionals are choosing Java Classes in Pune to build practical, job-ready skills and stay competitive in today’s software industry. Java is still one of the best technologies to master if you want to work in software development. What’s New in Java Development? Technology changes fast, but Java continues to prove its value year after year. Java is still the best option for creating safe, dependable, and extensive applications, despite the emergence of more recent programming languages. In 2026, the language is evolving with cloud-native development, AI integration, modern frameworks, and performance improvements that keep it relevant for today’s software industry. Whether you’re just starting your coding journey, preparing for a software career, or enhancing your expertise through Java Courses in Pune , understanding the latest Java trends can help you stay ahead of the competition. Institutions like 3RI Technologies have updated their training programs with real-world projects, up-to-date frameworks, and experiential learning that mirrors actual workplace challenges in order to support industry requirements. Why Java Technologies Still Matter in 2026 For years, Java has been trusted by businesses to build applications that are secure, scalable, and easy to maintain. Because of its adaptability, developers can produce anything from mobile solutions to cloud services and web apps. With constant innovation in java technologies , Java continues to meet the demands of modern software development while opening up exciting career opportunities for developers. Why businesses continue to select Java Platform-neutral “Write Once, Run Anywhere” functionality Robust security framework for business applications A sizable development community and frequent updates Outstanding assistance with cloud-native development Numerous Java library ecosystems and frameworks Simple integration with IoT, Big Data, and AI solutions Java Trends of 2026: Then vs Now Aspect Traditional Approach 2026 Trend Architecture Monolithic applications Microservices and modular design Deployment On-premise servers Cloud-native and serverless Concurrency Heavy platform threads Lightweight virtual threads Security Manual patching after release Automated, built-in security checks Training providers like 3RI Technologies have watched this demand play out up close, seeing more learners each year who want practical, job-ready Java skills instead of theory pulled from outdated course material. Top 10 Java Development Trends to Watch 1. Cloud-Native Java Development Is Becoming the Standard As more businesses move their applications to cloud platforms, Java developers are building software that is faster to deploy, easier to maintain, and capable of handling growing user demands. Cloud-native development has become one of the Top Java Development Trends because it allows organizations to release updates quickly while improving application reliability. Why it matters Supports scalable application development Works seamlessly with Docker and Kubernetes Reduces infrastructure costs Makes deployment and updates much faster Example: A banking application can automatically scale during peak transaction hours without affecting customer experience. 2. AI Is Expanding the Future of Java Applications Research initiatives are no longer the only uses for artificial intelligence. Today, developers are integrating AI into Java-based applications to deliver smarter user experiences and automate decision-making. This is one of the most exciting current trends in Java technology , especially for enterprise software. Common applications of AI Chatbots with intelligence Systems for detecting fraud Suggestion engines Solutions for predictive analytics Real-world example: Online shopping platforms use AI-powered recommendations developed with Java technologies to suggest products based on customer preferences. 3. Spring Boot Continues to Lead Enterprise Development Spring Boot continues to be the most popular Java framework for creating enterprise applications. It simplifies coding, speeds up development, and helps teams launch reliable applications with fewer configuration challenges. Key advantages Faster application development Easy REST API creation Strong security support Excellent microservices compatibility Many students joining Best Java Classes in Pune ​ begin with Spring Boot because it is widely used in the software industry. 4. Microservices Are Replacing Large Monolithic Applications Modern organizations are breaking large applications into smaller, independent services.
